{{< include ../_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}


This notebook reasons about time. It loads a small RDF knowledge graph of
Arretine ware findspots in the north-western Roman provinces and asks a
deceptively simple question: which sites were still in use when the *Clades
Variana* — the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 — took
place? Every code cell below runs in your browser; nothing is installed.
A companion Jupyter notebook, `clades_variana_temporal.ipynb`, contains the
same analysis for a local Python environment.

### Why this dataset?

The graph is deliberately small — 45 findspots, roughly 2,000 triples — but
unusually rich in temporal structure, which makes it a good vehicle for
OWL-Time. Three properties matter didactically. Each findspot carries an
explicit interval rather than a single date, so Allen's interval algebra has
something to work with. The intervals come from a published seriation, so they
are defensible rather than invented. And the same findspots are grouped twice
over: once computationally, once interpretively, which lets the same question
be asked of two different groupings and the answers compared.

### Data-context notes

Three things about this graph regularly trip people up.

*Two groupings, one graph.* A `lado:PeriodCluster` groups findspots that
received exactly the same start and end year from the seriation tool. A
`lado:ChronologicalHorizon` is the archaeological phase a findspot was
*assigned* to. The two are not interchangeable: horizons 1–3 happen to
coincide with a single cluster each, but horizon 4 absorbs three clusters and
horizon 5 two. A horizon's interval is therefore the *envelope* of its members
and can be wider than any single findspot in it.

*Astronomical year numbering.* Dates are `xsd:gYear` literals in the proleptic
Gregorian calendar, which includes a year zero. `"-0008"` is 9 BC, not 8 BC.
The helper `gyear_to_int` converts them; do not compare the literals directly.

*Fixed versus estimated boundaries.* `lado:startfixed` and `lado:endfixed`
mark boundaries resting on a historically dated event rather than on seriation
alone. Only seven findspots carry such an anchor, and they are what the whole
chronology hangs on.

### Tooling notes

The graph is parsed with `rdflib`, which is not bundled with Pyodide and is
installed with `micropip` in the first cell. Queries are plain SPARQL against
the in-memory graph, so no endpoint and no network round-trip is involved —
the Turtle file is shipped alongside this page and read straight from Pyodide's
virtual filesystem. Results are collected into `pandas` DataFrames, which is
pre-bundled.

Two charts at the end are drawn with hand-written HTML and JavaScript rather
than with `matplotlib`. In a browser notebook Python cannot touch the DOM, so
any interactive output has to be handed to the page as HTML; the local
companion notebook uses the identical HTML, just written to a file.

On first load, your browser downloads the Python runtime (Pyodide, ~10 MB) and

## 1 · Setup

`rdflib` is not part of the Pyodide bundle, so it is installed first. This is
the slowest cell in the notebook — a few seconds — and only needs to run once.

```{pyodide}

#| label: setup-micropip
import micropip
await micropip.install("rdflib")
print("\u2713 rdflib installed")
```

The Turtle file travels with this page (declared under `resources:` in the
front matter), so it is already present in Pyodide's virtual filesystem and can
be opened like any local file. The `pyfetch` branch is a fallback for the case
where the file was not copied into the VFS.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: load-graph
import warnings, logging
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
# rdflib logs xsd:gYear parse failures on some versions — silence during load
logging.disable(logging.CRITICAL)

import pandas as pd
from rdflib import Graph

TTL_NAME = "arretine_sites_minigraph.ttl"

try:                                  # normal path: file is in the Pyodide VFS
    with open(TTL_NAME, encoding="utf-8") as fh:
        ttl_text = fh.read()
except FileNotFoundError:             # fallback: fetch it over HTTP
    from pyodide.http import pyfetch
    ttl_text = await (await pyfetch(TTL_NAME)).string()

g = Graph()
g.parse(data=ttl_text, format="turtle")

logging.disable(logging.NOTSET)
print(f"Graph loaded: {len(g):,} triples from \"{TTL_NAME}\"")
```


## 2 · Helper Functions

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q2-helper-functions
def gyear_to_int(literal) -> int:
    """
    Convert an xsd:gYear RDF literal to a Python integer.

    xsd:gYear uses the proleptic Gregorian calendar in astronomical
    year numbering: '0009' = AD 9, '-0008' = 9 BC (there is no year 0
    in the historical calendar, but xsd:gYear includes it).
    """
    return int(str(literal))


def allen_relation(a0: int, a1: int, b0: int, b1: int) -> str:
    """
    Return the Allen interval relation of interval A = [a0, a1]
    with respect to interval B = [b0, b1].

    Implements all 13 basic relations from Allen (1983).
    """
    if   a1 < b0:                       return "before"
    elif a0 > b1:                       return "after"
    elif a1 == b0:                      return "meets"
    elif a0 == b1:                      return "metBy"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 == b1:         return "equals"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 > b1:          return "contains"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 < b1:          return "during"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 < b1:          return "starts"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 > b1:          return "startedBy"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 == b1:         return "finishedBy"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 == b1:         return "finishes"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 < b1:          return "overlaps"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 > b1:          return "overlappedBy"
    return "unknown"


# Relations representing 'after or concurrent with' the reference event.
# 'meets' is included: a site period ending exactly at AD 9
# was demonstrably active during the event (its final year coincides).
CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER = {
    "after",        # site begins after event ends
    "metBy",        # site begins exactly where event ends
    "equals",       # identical temporal extent
    "during",       # site falls entirely within event span
    "starts",       # site begins with event, ends earlier
    "startedBy",    # site begins with event, ends later
    "finishes",     # site ends with event, begins later
    "finishedBy",   # site ends with event, begins earlier
    "overlappedBy", # site begins before event ends, ends after
    "contains",     # site spans the entire event
    "meets",        # site ends exactly at event start (active in AD 9)
}
```

## 3 · Reference Event: *Clades Variana*

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q3-reference-event-clades-variana
q_event = """
    PREFIX ae:   <http://leiza-scit.github.io/CAA2026-alligator/>
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>

    SELECT ?label ?begin ?end
    WHERE {
        ae:event_Clades_Variana
            rdfs:label                        ?label ;
            time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?begin ;
            time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?end .
    }
"""

ev = list(g.query(q_event))[0]
EV_LABEL = str(ev[0])
EV_BEGIN = gyear_to_int(ev[1])
EV_END   = gyear_to_int(ev[2])

print(f"Reference event : {EV_LABEL}")
print(f"Temporal extent : AD {EV_BEGIN}\u2013AD {EV_END}  (point event)")
```

## 4 · Approach A: Absolute Temporal Comparison

All sites are retrieved via SPARQL. For each site, the Allen relation of its temporal
interval `[start, end]` to the *Clades Variana* interval `[9, 9]` is computed in Python.
Sites whose relation belongs to `CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER` are retained.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q4-approach-a-absolute-temporal
q_sites = """
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX fsl:  <http://fuzzy-sl.squirrel.link/ontology/>

    SELECT ?site ?label ?startYear ?endYear
    WHERE {
        ?site a time:Interval ;
              a fsl:Site ;
              rdfs:label                        ?label ;
              time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?startYear ;
              time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?endYear .
    }
    ORDER BY ?startYear ?label
"""

rows = []
for r in g.query(q_sites):
    s = gyear_to_int(r[2])
    e = gyear_to_int(r[3])
    rel = allen_relation(s, e, EV_BEGIN, EV_END)
    rows.append({
        "site_id":   str(r[0]).split("/")[-1],
        "label":     str(r[1]),
        "start":     s,
        "end":       e,
        "allen_rel": rel,
    })

df_all = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df_A = (
    df_all[df_all["allen_rel"].isin(CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER)]
    .sort_values(["allen_rel", "start", "label"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

print(f"Sites contemporary with or later than {EV_LABEL}: {len(df_A)} of {len(df_all)}")
print(f"\nRelation breakdown:")
print(df_A["allen_rel"].value_counts().to_string())
df_A
```

## 5 · Approach B: Relative Reasoning via Allen Relations on Cluster Level

The TTL dataset encodes explicit `time:interval*` relations between period *clusters*,
not between individual sites and events. We therefore:
1. Retrieve all clusters with their temporal extents and site memberships.
2. Compute the Allen relation of each cluster to the *Clades Variana* in Python.
3. Retain clusters (and their member sites) where the relation is in `CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER`.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q5-approach-b-relative-reasoning
q_clusters = """
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado: <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>

    SELECT ?cluster ?clusterLabel ?cBegin ?cEnd ?site ?siteLabel ?sBegin ?sEnd
    WHERE {
        ?cluster a lado:PeriodCluster ;
                 rdfs:label                        ?clusterLabel ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?cBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?cEnd ;
                 lado:hasClusterMember             ?site .

        ?site rdfs:label                        ?siteLabel ;
              time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?sBegin ;
              time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?sEnd .
    }
    ORDER BY ?clusterLabel ?siteLabel
"""

rows_b = []
for r in g.query(q_clusters):
    cb = gyear_to_int(r[2])
    ce = gyear_to_int(r[3])
    sb = gyear_to_int(r[6])
    se = gyear_to_int(r[7])
    cluster_rel = allen_relation(cb, ce, EV_BEGIN, EV_END)

    if cluster_rel in CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER:
        rows_b.append({
            "cluster":     str(r[1]),
            "c_start":     cb,
            "c_end":       ce,
            "cluster_rel": cluster_rel,
            "site":        str(r[5]),
            "site_start":  sb,
            "site_end":    se,
        })

df_B = (
    pd.DataFrame(rows_b)
    .sort_values(["cluster_rel", "c_start", "site"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

print(f"Qualifying sites (via cluster membership): {df_B['site'].nunique()} "
      f"across {df_B['cluster'].nunique()} clusters")
df_B
```

## 6 · Comparison: Approaches A and B

Both approaches should return identical site sets if the cluster membership
is consistent with the absolute date ranges in the data.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q6-comparison-approaches-a-and
sites_A = set(df_A["label"])
sites_B = set(df_B["site"])

print(f"Approach A (absolute) : {len(sites_A):>3} sites")
print(f"Approach B (relative) : {len(sites_B):>3} sites")
print(f"Intersection          : {len(sites_A & sites_B):>3} sites")

only_A = sites_A - sites_B
only_B = sites_B - sites_A
if only_A:
    print(f"\nOnly in A (not clustered): {sorted(only_A)}")
if only_B:
    print(f"\nOnly in B (cluster mis-match): {sorted(only_B)}")
if not only_A and not only_B:
    print("\n\u2713  Both approaches return identical site sets.")
```

## 7 · Cluster Overview — Allen Relations to the *Clades Variana*

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q7-cluster-overview-allen-relations
q_all_clusters = """
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado: <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>

    SELECT ?clusterLabel ?cBegin ?cEnd (COUNT(?site) AS ?nSites)
    WHERE {
        ?cluster a lado:PeriodCluster ;
                 rdfs:label                        ?clusterLabel ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?cBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?cEnd ;
                 lado:hasClusterMember             ?site .
    }
    GROUP BY ?clusterLabel ?cBegin ?cEnd
    ORDER BY ?cBegin
"""

rows_c = []
for r in g.query(q_all_clusters):
    cb = gyear_to_int(r[1])
    ce = gyear_to_int(r[2])
    rel = allen_relation(cb, ce, EV_BEGIN, EV_END)
    rows_c.append({
        "cluster":        str(r[0]),
        "start (CE/BCE)": cb,
        "end (CE/BCE)":   ce,
        "allen_rel":      rel,
        "sites":          int(str(r[3])),
        "included":       "\u2713" if rel in CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER else "\u2717",
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows_c).sort_values("start (CE/BCE)")
```

## 8 · Horizon Level: the Interpretive Grouping

The period clusters used above are **computed**: two findspots share a cluster when
Alligator assigned them exactly the same start and end year. The **chronological
horizons** are their archaeological counterpart — the phase a findspot has been
*assigned to* by the excavator's judgement (the table lives in `py/horizons.py`).

Both groupings are written into the same graph, so the identical Allen reasoning can
be applied to either:

| | Period cluster | Chronological horizon |
|---|---|---|
| Class | `lado:PeriodCluster` | `lado:ChronologicalHorizon`, `crm:E4_Period` |
| Membership | `lado:hasClusterMember` | `lado:hasHorizonMember` |
| Origin | computed from identical dates | interpretive assignment |
| Count | 8 | 5 |

A horizon's interval is the *envelope* of its findspots — earliest start to latest end.
Horizons 1–3 happen to coincide with a single cluster each; horizons 4 and 5 merge
three and two clusters respectively.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q8-horizon-level-the-interpretive
q_horizons = """
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado: <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>

    SELECT ?n ?horizonLabel ?hBegin ?hEnd (COUNT(?site) AS ?nSites)
    WHERE {
        ?horizon a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ;
                 skos:notation                     ?n ;
                 rdfs:label                        ?horizonLabel ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?hBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?hEnd ;
                 lado:hasHorizonMember             ?site .
        FILTER(langMatches(LANG(?horizonLabel), "en"))
    }
    GROUP BY ?n ?horizonLabel ?hBegin ?hEnd
    ORDER BY ?n
"""

rows_h = []
for r in g.query(q_horizons):
    hb = gyear_to_int(r[2])
    he = gyear_to_int(r[3])
    rel = allen_relation(hb, he, EV_BEGIN, EV_END)
    rows_h.append({
        "horizon":        str(r[1]),
        "start (CE/BCE)": hb,
        "end (CE/BCE)":   he,
        "allen_rel":      rel,
        "sites":          int(str(r[4])),
        "included":       "\u2713" if rel in CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER else "\u2717",
    })

pd.DataFrame(rows_h)
```

### 8.1 · Qualifying Sites via Horizon Membership

The same reasoning as approach B, but resolved over horizons instead of clusters: a
findspot qualifies when the horizon it belongs to is contemporary with, or later than,
the *Clades Variana*.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q8-1-qualifying-sites-via-horizon
q_horizon_sites = """
    PREFIX time: <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs: <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado: <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>

    SELECT ?n ?hBegin ?hEnd ?site ?siteLabel ?sBegin ?sEnd
    WHERE {
        ?horizon a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ;
                 skos:notation                     ?n ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?hBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?hEnd ;
                 lado:hasHorizonMember             ?site .

        ?site rdfs:label                        ?siteLabel ;
              time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?sBegin ;
              time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?sEnd .
    }
    ORDER BY ?n ?siteLabel
"""

rows_c = []
for r in g.query(q_horizon_sites):
    hb = gyear_to_int(r[1])
    he = gyear_to_int(r[2])
    horizon_rel = allen_relation(hb, he, EV_BEGIN, EV_END)

    if horizon_rel in CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER:
        rows_c.append({
            "horizon":     int(str(r[0])),
            "h_start":     hb,
            "h_end":       he,
            "horizon_rel": horizon_rel,
            "site":        str(r[4]),
            "site_start":  gyear_to_int(r[5]),
            "site_end":    gyear_to_int(r[6]),
        })

df_C = (
    pd.DataFrame(rows_c)
    .sort_values(["horizon", "site"])
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)

print(f"Qualifying sites (via horizon membership): {df_C['site'].nunique()} "
      f"across {df_C['horizon'].nunique()} horizons")
df_C
```

### 8.2 · Cluster Grouping vs Horizon Grouping

Do the computed and the interpretive grouping select the same findspots? Where they
differ, the reason is the coarser horizon envelope: a horizon spanning several clusters
inherits the *earliest* start and the *latest* end of its members, so a findspot can
qualify through its horizon that its own cluster would have excluded.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q8-2-cluster-grouping-vs-horizon
sites_B = set(df_B["site"])
sites_C = set(df_C["site"])

print(f"via clusters : {len(sites_B)}")
print(f"via horizons : {len(sites_C)}")
print(f"in both      : {len(sites_B & sites_C)}")

only_cluster = sorted(sites_B - sites_C)
only_horizon = sorted(sites_C - sites_B)

if only_cluster:
    print(f"\nonly via cluster ({len(only_cluster)}): {', '.join(only_cluster)}")
if only_horizon:
    print(f"\nonly via horizon ({len(only_horizon)}): {', '.join(only_horizon)}")
if not only_cluster and not only_horizon:
    print("\nBoth groupings select exactly the same findspots.")
```

## 9 · Working with the Horizons

Archaeologically the horizons carry more weight than the computed clusters: they are
the phases the material is actually discussed in. Now that they are first-class objects
in the graph, the questions an excavator asks can be put directly to SPARQL. The six
queries below stay on the horizon level throughout.

### 9.1 · Succession — Allen Relations Between the Horizons

The graph carries all 20 pairwise Allen relations between the five horizons, so the
sequence does not have to be read off a figure — it can be queried. The matrix below is
built entirely from `time:interval*` triples.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q9-1-succession-allen-relations-between
q_h_succession = """
    PREFIX time:      <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs:      <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado:      <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos:      <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
    PREFIX geosparql: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>

    SELECT ?a ?rel ?b
    WHERE {
        ?ha a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ; skos:notation ?a ; ?rel ?hb .
        ?hb a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ; skos:notation ?b .
        FILTER(STRSTARTS(STR(?rel), STR(time:)))
    }
    ORDER BY ?a ?b
"""

rel_rows = [
    {"A": int(r[0]),
      "relation": str(r[1]).split("#")[-1].replace("interval", ""),
      "B": int(r[2])}
    for r in g.query(q_h_succession)
]

matrix = (
    pd.DataFrame(rel_rows)
    .pivot(index="A", columns="B", values="relation")
    .fillna("\u2014")
)
matrix.index.name = "Horizon A"
matrix.columns.name = "Horizon B"
print("Read as: horizon A <relation> horizon B")
matrix
```

### 9.2 · Internal Structure — Which Findspots Do Not Fill Their Horizon?

A horizon's interval is the *envelope* of its members. Where every findspot carries the
same dating, the envelope describes the horizon exactly; where members differ, the
envelope is wider than any single findspot. This query separates the two cases and is
the quickest check of how homogeneous a horizon really is.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q9-2-internal-structure-which-findspots
q_h_members = """
    PREFIX time:      <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs:      <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado:      <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos:      <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
    PREFIX geosparql: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>

    SELECT ?n ?hBegin ?hEnd ?siteLabel ?sBegin ?sEnd
    WHERE {
        ?horizon a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ;
                 skos:notation                     ?n ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?hBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?hEnd ;
                 lado:hasHorizonMember             ?site .

        ?site rdfs:label                        ?siteLabel ;
              time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?sBegin ;
              time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?sEnd .
    }
    ORDER BY ?n ?siteLabel
"""

# The year comparison is done in Python: rdflib does not compare xsd:gYear
# literals with < / != the way a plain integer comparison would.
members = []
for r in g.query(q_h_members):
    hb, he = gyear_to_int(r[1]), gyear_to_int(r[2])
    sb, se = gyear_to_int(r[4]), gyear_to_int(r[5])
    members.append({
        "horizon":   int(str(r[0])),
        "h_start":   hb,
        "h_end":     he,
        "site":      str(r[3]),
        "s_start":   sb,
        "s_end":     se,
        "fills":     (sb, se) == (hb, he),
    })

df_members = pd.DataFrame(members)

summary = (
    df_members.groupby("horizon")
    .agg(sites=("site", "size"),
         fills_envelope=("fills", "sum"),
         narrower=("fills", lambda c: (~c).sum()))
    .reset_index()
)
print("Homogeneous horizons have every findspot filling the envelope:")
print(summary.to_string(index=False))

print("\nFindspots narrower than their horizon:")
df_members[~df_members["fills"]][["horizon", "site", "s_start", "s_end", "h_start", "h_end"]]
```

### 9.3 · Anchor Findspots — Historically Fixed Boundaries

Alligator marks a boundary as *fixed* when it rests on a historically dated event rather
than on seriation alone (`lado:startfixed` / `lado:endfixed`). These findspots anchor the
whole chronology, so it matters that every horizon contains at least one.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q9-3-anchor-findspots-historically-fixed
q_h_anchors = """
    PREFIX time:      <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs:      <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado:      <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos:      <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
```

## About this notebook

This notebook reasons about time. It loads a small RDF knowledge graph of
Arretine ware findspots in the north-western Roman provinces and asks a
deceptively simple question: which sites were still in use when the *Clades
Variana* — the loss of three legions in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 — took
place? Every code cell below runs in your browser; nothing is installed.
A companion Jupyter notebook, `clades_variana_temporal.ipynb`, contains the
same analysis for a local Python environment.

### Why this dataset?

The graph is deliberately small — 45 findspots, roughly 2,000 triples — but
unusually rich in temporal structure, which makes it a good vehicle for
OWL-Time. Three properties matter didactically. Each findspot carries an
explicit interval rather than a single date, so Allen's interval algebra has
something to work with. The intervals come from a published seriation, so they
are defensible rather than invented. And the same findspots are grouped twice
over: once computationally, once interpretively, which lets the same question
be asked of two different groupings and the answers compared.

### Data-context notes

Three things about this graph regularly trip people up.

*Two groupings, one graph.* A `lado:PeriodCluster` groups findspots that
received exactly the same start and end year from the seriation tool. A
`lado:ChronologicalHorizon` is the archaeological phase a findspot was
*assigned* to. The two are not interchangeable: horizons 1–3 happen to
coincide with a single cluster each, but horizon 4 absorbs three clusters and
horizon 5 two. A horizon's interval is therefore the *envelope* of its members
and can be wider than any single findspot in it.

*Astronomical year numbering.* Dates are `xsd:gYear` literals in the proleptic
Gregorian calendar, which includes a year zero. `"-0008"` is 9 BC, not 8 BC.
The helper `gyear_to_int` converts them; do not compare the literals directly.

*Fixed versus estimated boundaries.* `lado:startfixed` and `lado:endfixed`
mark boundaries resting on a historically dated event rather than on seriation
alone. Only seven findspots carry such an anchor, and they are what the whole
chronology hangs on.

### Tooling notes

The graph is parsed with `rdflib`, which is not bundled with Pyodide and is
installed with `micropip` in the first cell. Queries are plain SPARQL against
the in-memory graph, so no endpoint and no network round-trip is involved —
the Turtle file is shipped alongside this page and read straight from Pyodide's
virtual filesystem. Results are collected into `pandas` DataFrames, which is
pre-bundled.

Two charts at the end are drawn with hand-written HTML and JavaScript rather
than with `matplotlib`. In a browser notebook Python cannot touch the DOM, so
any interactive output has to be handed to the page as HTML; the local
companion notebook uses the identical HTML, just written to a file.

## 2 · Helper Functions

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q2-helper-functions
def gyear_to_int(literal) -> int:
    """
    Convert an xsd:gYear RDF literal to a Python integer.

    xsd:gYear uses the proleptic Gregorian calendar in astronomical
    year numbering: '0009' = AD 9, '-0008' = 9 BC (there is no year 0
    in the historical calendar, but xsd:gYear includes it).
    """
    return int(str(literal))


def allen_relation(a0: int, a1: int, b0: int, b1: int) -> str:
    """
    Return the Allen interval relation of interval A = [a0, a1]
    with respect to interval B = [b0, b1].

    Implements all 13 basic relations from Allen (1983).
    """
    if   a1 < b0:                       return "before"
    elif a0 > b1:                       return "after"
    elif a1 == b0:                      return "meets"
    elif a0 == b1:                      return "metBy"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 == b1:         return "equals"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 > b1:          return "contains"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 < b1:          return "during"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 < b1:          return "starts"
    elif a0 == b0 and a1 > b1:          return "startedBy"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 == b1:         return "finishedBy"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 == b1:         return "finishes"
    elif a0 < b0  and a1 < b1:          return "overlaps"
    elif a0 > b0  and a1 > b1:          return "overlappedBy"
    return "unknown"


# Relations representing 'after or concurrent with' the reference event.
# 'meets' is included: a site period ending exactly at AD 9
# was demonstrably active during the event (its final year coincides).
CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER = {
    "after",        # site begins after event ends
    "metBy",        # site begins exactly where event ends
    "equals",       # identical temporal extent
    "during",       # site falls entirely within event span
    "starts",       # site begins with event, ends earlier
    "startedBy",    # site begins with event, ends later
    "finishes",     # site ends with event, begins later
    "finishedBy",   # site ends with event, begins earlier
    "overlappedBy", # site begins before event ends, ends after
    "contains",     # site spans the entire event
    "meets",        # site ends exactly at event start (active in AD 9)
}
```

The TTL dataset encodes explicit `time:interval*` relations between period *clusters*,
not between individual sites and events. We therefore:
1. Retrieve all clusters with their temporal extents and site memberships.
2. Compute the Allen relation of each cluster to the *Clades Variana* in Python.
3. Retain clusters (and their member sites) where the relation is in `CONTEMPORARY_OR_LATER`.

## 8 · Horizon Level: the Interpretive Grouping

The period clusters used above are **computed**: two findspots share a cluster when
Alligator assigned them exactly the same start and end year. The **chronological
horizons** are their archaeological counterpart — the phase a findspot has been
*assigned to* by the excavator's judgement (the table lives in `py/horizons.py`).

Both groupings are written into the same graph, so the identical Allen reasoning can
be applied to either:

| | Period cluster | Chronological horizon |
|---|---|---|
| Class | `lado:PeriodCluster` | `lado:ChronologicalHorizon`, `crm:E4_Period` |
| Membership | `lado:hasClusterMember` | `lado:hasHorizonMember` |
| Origin | computed from identical dates | interpretive assignment |
| Count | 8 | 5 |

A horizon's interval is the *envelope* of its findspots — earliest start to latest end.
Horizons 1–3 happen to coincide with a single cluster each; horizons 4 and 5 merge
three and two clusters respectively.

```{pyodide}

    PREFIX skos: <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>

    SELECT ?n ?horizonLabel ?hBegin ?hEnd (COUNT(?site) AS ?nSites)
    WHERE {
        ?horizon a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ;
                 skos:notation                     ?n ;
                 rdfs:label                        ?horizonLabel ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?hBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?hEnd ;
                 lado:hasHorizonMember             ?site .
        FILTER(langMatches(LANG(?horizonLabel), "en"))
    }
    GROUP BY ?n ?horizonLabel ?hBegin ?hEnd

"""

    he = gyear_to_int(r[3])
```

## 9 · Working with the Horizons

Archaeologically the horizons carry more weight than the computed clusters: they are
the phases the material is actually discussed in. Now that they are first-class objects
in the graph, the questions an excavator asks can be put directly to SPARQL. The six
queries below stay on the horizon level throughout.

### 9.1 · Succession — Allen Relations Between the Horizons

The graph carries all 20 pairwise Allen relations between the five horizons, so the
sequence does not have to be read off a figure — it can be queried. The matrix below is

### 9.2 · Internal Structure — Which Findspots Do Not Fill Their Horizon?

A horizon's interval is the *envelope* of its members. Where every findspot carries the
same dating, the envelope describes the horizon exactly; where members differ, the
envelope is wider than any single findspot. This query separates the two cases and is
the quickest check of how homogeneous a horizon really is.

```{pyodide}
#| autorun: false
#| label: q9-2-internal-structure-which-findspots

    PREFIX time:      <http://www.w3.org/2006/time#>
    PREFIX rdfs:      <http://www.w3.org/2000/01/rdf-schema#>
    PREFIX lado:      <http://archaeology.link/ontology#>
    PREFIX skos:      <http://www.w3.org/2004/02/skos/core#>
    PREFIX geosparql: <http://www.opengis.net/ont/geosparql#>

    SELECT ?n ?hBegin ?hEnd ?siteLabel ?sBegin ?sEnd
    WHERE {
        ?horizon a lado:ChronologicalHorizon ;
                 skos:notation                     ?n ;
                 time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?hBegin ;
                 time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?hEnd ;
                 lado:hasHorizonMember             ?site .

        ?site rdfs:label                        ?siteLabel ;
              time:hasBeginning/time:inXSDgYear ?sBegin ;
              time:hasEnd/time:inXSDgYear       ?sEnd .
    }
    ORDER BY ?n ?siteLabel
"""

# The year comparison is done in Python: rdflib does not compare xsd:gYear
# literals with < / != the way a plain integer comparison would.
members = []
for r in g.query(q_h_members):
    hb, he = gyear_to_int(r[1]), gyear_to_int(r[2])
    sb, se = gyear_to_int(r[4]), gyear_to_int(r[5])
    members.append({
        "horizon":   int(str(r[0])),
        "h_start":   hb,
        "h_end":     he,
        "site":      str(r[3]),
        "s_start":   sb,
        "s_end":     se,
        "fills":     (sb, se) == (hb, he),
    })

df_members = pd.DataFrame(members)

summary = (
    df_members.groupby("horizon")
    .agg(sites=("site", "size"),
         fills_envelope=("fills", "sum"),
         narrower=("fills", lambda c: (~c).sum()))
    .reset_index()
)
print("Homogeneous horizons have every findspot filling the envelope:")
print(summary.to_string(index=False))

print("\nFindspots narrower than their horizon:")
df_members[~df_members["fills"]][["horizon", "site", "s_start", "s_end", "h_start", "h_end"]]
```
